We may use perturbation theory to compute the interface contribution to free energy at $d=4-\epsilon$ . Because the scalar field has Dirichlet boundary conditions, we require an additional integral beyond (4.36), which we denote $I_{2}$ :

$$ \begin{split}I_{2}(\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2},d)&\equiv\int d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\sqrt{g_{x_{1}}}\sqrt{g_{x_{2}}}\frac{1}{(4\xi_{12})^{\Delta_{1}}}\frac{1}{(4(\xi_{12}+1))^{\Delta_{2}}}\\
&=\text{vol}(H^{d})\Omega_{d-1}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\eta(\sinh(\eta))^{d-1}\frac{1}{(4\sinh^{2}(\eta/2))^{\Delta_{1}}(4\cosh^{2}(\eta/2))^{\Delta_{2}}}\\
&=\frac{\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}+\frac{d}{2}}2^{d-2\Delta_{1}-2\Delta_{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}-\Delta_{1}\right)\Gamma\left(-d+\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+1\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta_{2}+1\right)}.\end{split} $$

Thus, the free energy contribution to from the interaction is, to leading order,

$$ \begin{split}F_{\rm int}^{GNY}&=-\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{2}\int d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\sqrt{g_{x_{1}}}\sqrt{g_{x_{2}}}\langle s\bar{\psi}_{i}\psi^{i}(x_{1})s\bar{\psi}_{i}\psi^{i}(x_{2})\rangle\\
&=-\frac{N\epsilon}{2(N+6)\pi^{4}}\int d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\sqrt{g_{x_{1}}}\sqrt{g_{x_{2}}}\frac{1}{(4\xi)^{d-1}}\left(\frac{1}{(4\xi)^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}-\frac{1}{(4(1+\xi))^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}\right)\\
&=-\frac{N\epsilon}{2\pi^{4}(N+6)}\left(I_{1}(\tfrac{3d}{2}-2,4-\epsilon)-I_{2}(d-1,\tfrac{d}{2}-1,4-\epsilon)\right)\\
&=\frac{N\epsilon}{96(N+2)}\xrightarrow{\text{Large }N}\frac{\epsilon}{96}\end{split} $$

Note that the contribution from the $I_{2}$ integral is actually zero due to the $\Gamma(0)$ in the denominator of (4.50), so computing the $F_{\rm int}^{GNY}$ with the Dirichlet propagator for $\sigma$ yields the same result as using the $\sigma$ propagator with no boundary condition.

To see how this provides a check of the large $N$ result $F_{\sigma}(\Delta)$ , note that the IR fixed point of the GNY model is expected to be equivalent to the CFT at the UV fixed point of the GN model [58]. In other words, we expect the following to be true

$$ F_{GNY}|_{g_{1}^{*},g_{2}^{*}}=F_{GN}|_{g^{*}}=N_{f}F_{f}+F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-1)+O(1/N) $$

and by comparing the above equation to (4.49), we see that $F_{\rm int}^{GNY}$ should be related to $F_{\sigma}$ as

$$ F_{\rm int}^{GNY}=F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-1)-F_{s}^{D}. $$

We first obtain $F_{\sigma}$ by plugging in $\Delta=d-1$ and $d=4-\epsilon$ into (3.18):

$$ \begin{split}F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-1)&=\frac{1}{\Gamma(d+1)\sin(\pi d)}\int_{0}^{1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}}du\ u\ \Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}+u\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}-u\right)\sin\pi\left(\frac{d}{2}-u\right)\\
&\overset{d\to 4-\epsilon}{=}\frac{1}{180\epsilon}+\frac{240\log(A)-480\zeta^{\prime}(-3)-\frac{180\zeta(3)}{\pi^{2}}-29-16\gamma}{2880}+0.00727\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{2})\end{split} $$

where $A$ is Glaisher’s constant and $\gamma$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. To obtain $F_{s}^{D}$ , note that the free energy of the scalar on the whole sphere, $F_{s}$ , is given by summing over Dirichlet and Neumann modes:

$$ F_{s}=F_{s}^{D}+F_{s}^{N}=-\frac{1}{\sin(\pi d/2)\Gamma(1+d)}\int_{0}^{1}du\ u\sin(\pi u)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}+u\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}-u\right) $$

where $F_{s}$ is given in [57]. On the other hand, the change in free energy flowing from Neumann to Dirichlet boundary conditions is given by [51]

$$ F_{s}^{N}-F_{s}^{D}=-\frac{1}{\sin(\tfrac{\pi(d-1)}{2})\Gamma(d)}\int_{0}^{\tfrac{1}{2}}du\ u\sin(\pi u)\Gamma\left(\frac{d-1}{2}+u\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d-1}{2}-u\right). $$

So the free energy contribution from the scalar on the hemisphere with Dirichlet boundary conditions is just

$$ \begin{split}F_{s}^{D}&=\frac{1}{2}(F_{s}-(F_{s}^{N}-F_{s}^{D}))\\
&\overset{d\to 4-\epsilon}{=}\frac{1}{180\epsilon}+\frac{240\log(A)-480\zeta^{\prime}(-3)-29-16\gamma}{2880}-\frac{\zeta(3)}{16\pi^{2}}-0.003149\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{2}).\end{split} $$

Then, according to (4.53), we find that the contribution from the GNY interaction term at large $N$ , specified to $d=4-\epsilon$ should be

$$ F_{\rm int}^{GNY}=F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-1)-F_{s}^{D}=\frac{\epsilon}{96}+O(\epsilon^{2}), $$

in agreement with the epsilon expansion result.

### 4.4 Cubic $O(N)$ model

We now consider the cubic $O(N)$ scalar theory given by

$$ S=\int d^{d}x\left(\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{\mu}\phi^{i})^{2}+\ \theta(z)\left(\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{\mu}s)^{2}+\frac{g_{1}}{2}s\phi^{i}\phi^{i}+\frac{g_{2}}{6}s^{3}\right)\right). $$

For $N>N_{crit}$ , the interacting model has unitary IR stable perturbative fixed points at $d=6-\epsilon$ . At leading order in large $N$ , the couplings at the fixed point are given by [60]

$$ \begin{split}g_{1}^{*}&=\sqrt{\frac{6\epsilon(4\pi)^{3}}{N}}\\
g_{2}^{*}&=6g_{1}^{*}.\end{split} $$

#### 4.4.1 Free energy

The free energy of the theory is given by

$$ F_{\text{cubic }O(N)}=NF_{s}+F_{s}^{D}+F_{\rm int}^{\text{cubic }O(N)} $$

Using ordinary perturbation theory at $d=6-\epsilon$ , we compute the contribution to the free energy from the interaction term, which gives

$$ \begin{split}F_{\rm int}^{\text{cubic }O(N)}&=-\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{8}\int d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\langle s\phi^{i}\phi^{i}(x_{1})s\phi^{i}\phi^{i}(x_{2})\rangle\\
&=-\frac{3\epsilon}{2\pi^{6}}\int d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\sqrt{g_{x_{1}}}\sqrt{g_{x_{2}}}\frac{1}{(4\xi)^{d-2}}\left(\frac{1}{(4\xi)^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}-\frac{1}{(4(1+\xi))^{\frac{d}{2}-1}}\right)\\
&=-\frac{3\epsilon}{2\pi^{6}}\left(I_{1}(\tfrac{3d}{2}-3,6-\epsilon)-I_{2}(d-2,\tfrac{d}{2}-1,6-\epsilon)\right)\\
&=-\frac{\epsilon}{960}+O(\epsilon^{2}).\end{split} $$

Though we imposed Dirichlet boundary conditions on $\sigma$ , we again find that the contribution from the $I_{2}$ integral is zero due to the $\Gamma(0)$ in the denominator of (4.50).

To provide a check of the large $N$ result $F_{\sigma}(\Delta)$ , note that the IR fixed point of the cubic $O(N)$ model is equivalent to the CFT at the UV fixed point of the $O(N)$ model [60]. Thus, we expect

$$ F_{\text{cubic }O(N)}|_{g_{1}^{*},g_{2}^{*}}=F_{O(N)}|_{\lambda^{*}}=NF_{s}+F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-2)+O(1/N) $$

and by comparing this to (4.61), we see $F_{\rm int}^{\text{cubic }O(N)}$ can be expressed in terms of $F_{\sigma}$ as

$$ F_{\rm int}^{GNY}=F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-2)-F_{s}^{D}. $$

We first obtain $F_{\sigma}$ by plugging in $\Delta=d-2$ and $d=6-\epsilon$ to (3.18):

$$ \begin{split}F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-2)&=\frac{1}{\Gamma(d+1)\sin(\pi d)}\int_{0}^{1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}}du\ u\ \Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}+u\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}-u\right)\sin\pi\left(\frac{d}{2}-u\right)\\
&\overset{d\to 6-\epsilon}{=}-\frac{1}{1512\epsilon}+\frac{-378\log(A)-378\zeta^{\prime}(-5)+47+30\gamma}{45360}+\frac{\zeta(5)}{64\pi^{4}}+\frac{\zeta(3)}{192\pi^{2}}\\
&\qquad-0.000835423\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{2}).\end{split} $$

The free energy contribution from a free scalar on the hemisphere with Dirichlet boundary conditions was found in (4.3), and in $d=6-\epsilon$ it is given by

$$ \begin{split}F_{s}^{D}&\underset{d=6-\epsilon}{=}-\frac{1}{1512\epsilon}+\frac{-378\log(A)-378\zeta^{\prime}(-5)+47+30\gamma}{45360}+\frac{\zeta(5)}{64\pi^{4}}+\frac{\zeta(3)}{192\pi^{2}}\\
&\qquad+0.000206243817\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{2}).\end{split} $$

Thus, we have

$$ \delta F^{\text{cubic }O(N)}=F_{\sigma}(\Delta=d-2)-F_{s}^{D}=-\frac{\epsilon}{960}+O(\epsilon^{2}), $$

again in agreement with the epsilon expansion result.

## 5 Holographic setup

In this section we review the holographic dual of the large $N$ double trace interface discussed in [21]. This is essentially a generalization of the well-known dictionary [22] relating double-trace deformations to alternate boundary conditions in AdS. A schematic summary of the setup is shown in Figure 1. In the next section we will then apply these results to show equivalence between AdS and CFT calculations of various correlation functions.

Following [21], it is convenient to use the following Janus coordinates for the $H^{d+1}$ bulk99 9 An alternative, perhaps more familiar, form of the metric is obtained by setting $w=\frac{1}{2}(1+\tanh(\rho))$ , which gives $ds^{2}_{H^{d+1}}=d\rho^{2}+\cosh^{2}\rho\,ds^{2}_{H^{d}}$ , where $-\infty<\rho<\infty$ and the two $H^{d}$ boundaries are at $\rho=\pm\infty$ .

$$ ds_{H^{d+1}}^{2}=\frac{dw^{2}}{4w^{2}(1-w)^{2}}+\frac{ds^{2}_{H^{d}}}{4w(1-w)},\qquad w\in(0,1) $$

where $H^{d+1}$ is foliated by $H^{d}$ slices, and the two $H^{d}$ boundary slices at $w=0$ and $w=1$ are expected to respectively correspond, upon Weyl rescaling, to the half-spaces where the UV and IR CFTs live. The interface is at the boundary of $H^{d}$ (this is the common boundary of the two halves of the $H^{d+1}$ boundary).

*Figure 1: Schematic depiction of the holographic setup describing the double-trace interfaces. The boundary of $H^{d+1}$ is divided into two $H^{d}$ regions, which correspond to the (Weyl-rescaled) left and right halves of the interface CFT. The bulk scalar field $\varphi$ dual to the operator $O$ has inhomogeneous boundary conditions corresponding to dual dimension $\Delta$ near the left (black) boundary, and to dual dimension $d-\Delta$ near the right (red) boundary. The two $H^{d}$ regions are joined through their common boundary, which corresponds to the interface on the CFT side.*

We denote $X=(w,x)\in H^{d+1}$ where $x\in H^{d}$ can be written in Poincare coordinates as in (3.3). We will use the notation $\langle\dots\rangle_{H^{d}}$ to denote correlation functions in the Weyl-rescaled CFTs, i.e. $\langle O(x)O(x^{\prime})\rangle_{H^{d}}=z^{\Delta}(z^{\prime})^{\Delta}\langle O(x)O(x^{\prime})\rangle$ .

In the absence of the interface, the bulk scalar field $\varphi$ dual to the operator $O$ has the standard bulk propagator $G_{\Delta}(X,X^{\prime})$ on a pure AdS background, satisfying the equation

$$ (-\nabla^{2}_{H^{d+1}}+m^{2})G_{\Delta}(X,X^{\prime})=\delta(X,X^{\prime}) $$

and with the following homogeneous boundary conditions ( $\sim(w^{\prime})^{\Delta/2}$ or $(1-w^{\prime})^{\Delta/2}$ )1010 10 These boundary conditions describe the “UV CFT” where $O$ has scaling dimension $\Delta$ . The case of homogeneous boundary conditions with $\Delta\rightarrow d-\Delta$ would describe the double-trace deformation turned on over the full space. in terms of Janus coordinates as $w^{\prime}\to 0$ and $w^{\prime}\to 1$ :

$$ \begin{split}G_{\Delta}(X;w^{\prime},x^{\prime})&=\begin{cases}-\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}K_{\Delta}(X;x^{\prime})(4w^{\prime})^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+O(w^{\prime\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}})&w^{\prime}\to 0\\
-\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}K_{\Delta}(X;x^{\prime})(4(1-w^{\prime}))^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+O((1-w^{\prime})^{(\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}})&w^{\prime}\to 1\end{cases}.\end{split} $$

Above, $K_{\Delta}$ is the standard scalar bulk-to-boundary propagator, given in Janus coordinates by

$$ K_{\Delta}(w,x;x^{\prime})=\begin{cases}\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{w(1-w)}}{2(w+\xi)}\right)^{\Delta},&w^{\prime}=0\\
\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{w(1-w)}}{2(1-w+\xi)}\right)^{\Delta},&w^{\prime}=1\end{cases} $$

where the normalization constant is

$$ \mathcal{C}_{\Delta}=\frac{\Gamma(\Delta)}{\pi^{d/2}\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)}\,. $$

In these conventions for the bulk-to-boundary propagator, the two-point function of the dual CFT operator (in the absence of the interface) is given by $\langle O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle_{0}=(2\Delta-d)\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}/x_{12}^{2\Delta}$ [61, 22]. This means that in these conventions, we can identify $C_{O}=(2\Delta-d)\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}$ , where $C_{O}$ is the two-point normalization constant defined in (2.5).

In the presence of the double trace interface, one should instead impose inhomogeneous boundary conditions on the bulk scalar field, corresponding to dual dimension $\Delta$ or $d-\Delta$ in the left and right half of the boundary, respectively. The corresponding Green’s function, denoted $\tilde{G}$ below, satisfies the usual equation

$$ (-\nabla^{2}_{H^{d+1}}+m^{2})\tilde{G}(X,X^{\prime})=\delta(X,X^{\prime}) $$

but now with different asymptotics (either $\sim(w^{\prime})^{\Delta/2}$ or $\sim(1-w^{\prime})^{(d-\Delta)/2}$ ) as one point of the propagator is sent towards the $w^{\prime}=0$ or $w^{\prime}=1$ $H^{d}$ slice:

$$ \begin{split}&\tilde{G}(X;w^{\prime},x^{\prime})\\
&=\begin{cases}-\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}(X;x^{\prime})(4w^{\prime})^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+0\cdot(w^{\prime})^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O((w^{\prime})^{\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}}),&w^{\prime}\to 0\\
0\cdot(1-w^{\prime})^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}(X;x^{\prime})(4(1-w^{\prime}))^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O((1-w^{\prime})^{\tfrac{d-\Delta+2}{2}}),&w^{\prime}\to 1\end{cases}.\end{split} $$

Above, the bulk-to-boundary propagators1111 11 In the notation of [21], $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ corresponds to “ $K_{L}^{-+}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ ” and $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ corresponds to “ $K_{R}^{-+}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ ”. $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ and $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ depend on whether the boundary insertion is at $w^{\prime}=0$ or $w^{\prime}=1$ :

$$ \begin{split}\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}(w,x;x^{\prime})&=\dfrac{\sin\pi(\Delta-\tfrac{d}{2})}{\pi}\dfrac{\Gamma(\tfrac{d}{2})}{\pi^{d/2}}\dfrac{[4w(1-w)]^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}}{4^{\Delta}(1-w)^{\Delta-d/2}}(1+\xi)^{-\tfrac{d}{2}}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(1,\frac{d}{2},1+\tfrac{d}{2}-\Delta;\dfrac{1-w}{1+\xi}\right)\\
\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}(w,x;x^{\prime})&=\dfrac{\sin\pi(\tfrac{d}{2}-\Delta)}{\pi}\dfrac{\Gamma(\tfrac{d}{2})}{\pi^{d/2}}\dfrac{[4w(1-w)]^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}}{4^{d-\Delta}w^{d/2-\Delta}}(1+\xi)^{-\tfrac{d}{2}}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(1,\tfrac{d}{2},\Delta-\tfrac{d}{2}+1;\dfrac{w}{1+\xi}\right).\end{split} $$

Note that we can go from $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ to $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}(w,x;x^{\prime})$ by taking $w\to 1-w$ and $\Delta\to d-\Delta$ . The bulk propagator $\tilde{G}(X;X^{\prime})$ solved for in [21] takes a complicated form that we include in Appendix C. The asymptotics of $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}$ and $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}$ as we take $w\to 0,1$ are related to the various two-point functions involving the operators $O$ (of dimension $\Delta$ ) and $\sigma$ (of dimension $d-\Delta$ ) in the dual CFT. For example, the $w\to 0$ limit of $\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=0}$ is given by

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{w\to 0}&\tilde{K}_{w_{L}=0}(x_{L};w,x)=-(4w)^{\Delta/2}\frac{\Gamma(\tfrac{d}{2})\sin(\tfrac{\pi(d-2\Delta)}{2})}{\pi^{\frac{d}{2}+1}(\xi+1)^{d/2}}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,\frac{d}{2};\frac{d}{2}-\Delta+1;\frac{1}{\xi+1}\right)+O(w^{\Delta/2+1})\\
&=-(4w)^{\Delta/2}\frac{\Gamma(\tfrac{d}{2})\sin(\tfrac{\pi(d-2\Delta)}{2})}{\pi^{\frac{d}{2}+1}(\xi)^{d/2}}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{d}{2},\frac{d}{2}-\Delta;\frac{d}{2}-\Delta+1;-\frac{1}{\xi}\right)+O(w^{\Delta/2+1})\\
&=(4w)^{\Delta/2}\frac{z_{1}^{\Delta}z_{2}^{\Delta}\langle O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle}{2\Delta-d}+O(w^{\Delta/2+1})\end{split} $$

where we applied a hypergeometric identity1212 12 $\,{}_{2}F_{1}(a,b,c,z)=(1-z)^{-b}\,_{2}F_{1}(c-a,b,c,\frac{z}{z-1})$ in the second line. To get the last line, we recall that the normalization conventions we are using on the AdS side correspond to the choice $C_{O}=(2\Delta-d)\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}$ , as explained below (5.5). The rest of the asymptotics are obtained in a similar way:

$$ \begin{split}&\tilde{K}_{w_{L}=0}(x_{L};w,x)\\
=&\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2\Delta-d}\langle O(x_{L})O(x)\rangle_{H^{d}}(4w)^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+\delta(x-x^{\prime})(4w)^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O(w^{\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}}),&w\to 0\\
0\cdot(1-w)^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}-\langle\sigma(x)O(x_{L})\rangle_{H^{d}}^{\text{folded}}(4(1-w))^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O((1-w)^{\tfrac{d-\Delta+2}{2}}),&w\to 1\end{cases}\\
&\tilde{K}_{w_{R}=1}(w,x;x_{R})\\
=&\begin{cases}\langle O(x)\sigma(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}^{\text{folded}}(4w)^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+0\cdot w^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O(w^{\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}}),&w\to 0\\
\delta(x-x^{\prime})(4(1-w))^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}-(2\Delta-d)\langle\sigma(x)\sigma(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}(4(1-w))^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O((1-w)^{\tfrac{d-\Delta+2}{2}}),&w\to 1\end{cases}.\end{split} $$

One can see that the two-point functions defined by the above limits of the bulk-boundary propagator (5.8) indeed agree with those computed in Section 2 using the large $N$ expansion on the CFT side. In the expressions above, we introduced the “folded” superscript to denote correlators that differ as a function of $\xi$ when going from the folded to the unfolded theory, so it is only necessary to include when the corresponding flat space correlation function contains operators on opposite sides of the interface. For example, in the UV theory we have

$$ \begin{split}\langle O(\mathbf{x}_{1},z_{1})O(\mathbf{x}_{2},z_{2})\rangle_{0,H^{d}}&=C_{O}(4\xi)^{-\Delta},\qquad\text{sign}(z_{1}z_{2})=1\\
\langle O(\mathbf{x}_{1},z_{1})O(\mathbf{x}_{2},z_{2})\rangle_{0,H^{d}}^{\text{folded}}&=C_{O}(-4\xi)^{-\Delta}\bigg|_{z_{1}\to-z_{1}}=C_{O}(4(1+\xi))^{-\Delta},\qquad\text{sign}(z_{1}z_{2})=-1.\end{split} $$

For comparison with $\tilde{K}$ , we also write the asymptotics of the standard bulk-to-boundary propagator $K_{\Delta}$ :

$$ \begin{split}&K_{\Delta}(w,x;w^{\prime},x^{\prime})\\
&=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2\Delta-d}\langle O(x^{\prime})O(x)\rangle_{0,H^{d}}(4w)^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+\delta(x-x^{\prime})(4w)^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O(w^{\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}}),&w^{\prime}=0,w\to 0\\
\frac{1}{2\Delta-d}\langle O(x^{\prime})O(x)\rangle_{0,H^{d}}^{\text{folded}}(4(1-w))^{\tfrac{\Delta}{2}}+0\cdot(1-w)^{\tfrac{d-\Delta}{2}}+O((1-w)^{\tfrac{\Delta+2}{2}}),&w^{\prime}=0,w\to 1.\\
\end{cases}\end{split} $$

With an explicit expression for the bulk propagator at coincident points $\tilde{G}(X;X)$ , one can compute the one-loop correction to the free energy on the sphere. This is calculated in [21] as

$$ \begin{split}&\frac{(F-F_{0,\text{UV}})+(F-F_{0,\text{IR}})}{2}=-\log\left(\frac{\text{det}(-\nabla^{2}_{H^{d+1}}+m^{2})\left[\text{det}(-\nabla^{2}_{H^{d+1}}+m^{2})\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\to 1-w\\
\Delta\to d-\Delta\end{subarray}}}{\text{det}\left(-\nabla^{2}_{H^{d+1}}+m^{2}\right)_{0,\text{UV}}\text{det}\left(-\nabla^{2}_{H^{d+1}}+m^{2}\right)_{0,\text{IR}}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\\
&\frac{\partial}{\partial m^{2}}\left[\frac{(F-F_{0,\text{UV}})+(F-F_{0,\text{IR}})}{2}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\int d^{d+1}X\sqrt{g_{H^{d+1}}}\biggr[\tilde{G}_{\Delta}(X;X)+\tilde{G}_{d-\Delta}(X;X)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-G_{\Delta}(X;X)-G_{d-\Delta}(X;X)\biggr]\end{split} $$

where, as in Section 3.1, we explicitly write the “UV” subscript to distinguish the UV and IR theories on the full sphere. As discussed in Section 3.1, the above AdS calculation matches our large $N$ CFT result in Eq. (3.21).

## 6 Equivalence of CFT and AdS calculations

In this section, we will show there is a manifest equivalence between calculations of correlation functions in the $H^{d+1}$ bulk and those in the interface CFT. As in the simpler case of a double-trace deformation over the whole space [28, 34, 30], the equivalence follows from certain identities involving the bulk two-point functions and bulk-to-boundary propagators discussed in the previous section. We begin by describing the identities, then proceed to apply them to the explicit examples of one-point and three-point functions to show the equivalence of AdS and CFT calculations. The extension to general correlation functions should follow along similar lines.

### 6.1 Identity for $\tilde{G}-G_{\Delta}$

As pointed out in [21], the difference $\tilde{G}-G_{\Delta}$ can be expressed as a convolution on the boundary between $K_{\Delta}$ and a function proportional to $\tilde{K}_{w=1}$ :

$$ \tilde{G}(w_{1},x_{1};w_{2},x_{2})-G_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};w_{2},x_{2})=\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x^{\prime}K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x^{\prime})\tilde{K}_{w^{\prime}=1}(w_{2},x_{2};x^{\prime}). $$

This identity is depicted diagrammatically in Figure 2.

*Figure 2: Diagrammatic representation of (6.1)*

To prove the identity, one can notice that each side of (6.1) satisfies the scalar equation of motion in the $H^{d+1}$ bulk (this is immediate to see), and has the same boundary conditions. To see the matching boundary conditions, we can take $w_{2}\to 0$ using the asymptotic expressions given in (5.7), (5.3), (5.10), and (5.12), which gives

$$ w_{2}\to 0 \displaystyle LHS(\ref{eq:GIdentity})\to w_{2}^{\Delta/2}\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}\left(-\tilde{K}_{w_{2}=0}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2})+K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2})\right) \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+w_{2}^{(d-\Delta)/2}\cdot 0+\dots \displaystyle RHS(\ref{eq:GIdentity})\to w_{2}^{\Delta/2}\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x^{\prime}\sqrt{g}K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x^{\prime})\langle\sigma(x^{\prime})O(x_{2})\rangle_{H^{d}} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+w_{2}^{(d-\Delta)/2}\cdot 0+\dots $$

where one only needs the vanishing $w_{2}^{(d-\Delta)/2}$ asymptotics to specify boundary conditions. Similarly, taking $w_{2}\to 1$ gives1313 13 Again, when we write bulk results in terms of CFT correlators, we specialize to the normalization choice $C_{O}=(2\Delta-d)\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}$ , which follows from our bulk-to-boundary propagator conventions.

$$ w_{2}\to 1 \displaystyle LHS(\ref{eq:GIdentity})\to(1-w_{2})^{\Delta/2}\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2}) \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+(1-w_{2})^{(d-\Delta)/2}\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}\tilde{K}_{w_{2}=1}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2})+\dots \displaystyle RHS(\ref{eq:GIdentity})\to(1-w_{2})^{\Delta/2}\frac{1}{d-2\Delta}K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2}) \displaystyle\qquad(1-w_{2})^{(d-\Delta)/2}\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x^{\prime}\sqrt{g}K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x^{\prime})\langle\sigma(x_{2})\sigma(x^{\prime})\rangle_{H^{d}}+\dots $$

where one only needs the $(1-w_{2})^{\Delta/2}$ asymptotics to specify boundary conditions. Clearly there are matching boundary conditions for each side of (6.1), verifying the validity of the expression. In addition, by matching the coefficients of $w_{2}^{\Delta/2}$ as $w_{2}\to 0$ and $(1-w_{2})^{(d-\Delta)/2}$ as $w_{2}\to 1$ , we arrive at two identities relating $\tilde{K}$ to a convolution on the boundary between $K_{\Delta}$ and a CFT correlator:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{K}_{w_{2}=0}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2}) \displaystyle=K^{w_{2}=0}_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2})-\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x^{\prime}\sqrt{g}K^{w^{\prime}=1}_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x^{\prime})\langle\sigma(x^{\prime})O(x_{2})\rangle_{H^{d}} \displaystyle\tilde{K}_{w_{2}=1}(w_{1},x_{1};x_{2}) \displaystyle=\ (d-2\Delta)\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x^{\prime}\sqrt{g}K^{w^{\prime}=1}_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};x^{\prime})\langle\sigma(x^{\prime})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle_{H^{d}}. $$

### 6.2 One-point functions

#### 6.2.1 $\langle\Phi\rangle$

We now discuss the holographic computation of one-point functions for various operators. In Section 2.1 we considered the one-point function coefficients of $\Phi$ , an operator other than $O$ or $\sigma$ , when inserted on either the UV or IR side of the interface. In the $H^{d+1}$ bulk, the (Weyl-rescaled) one-point function for $\Phi$ inserted on the IR (“right”) side of the interface is given to leading order by a one-loop tadpole Witten diagram

$$ \begin{split}\langle\Phi(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}&=\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{TadpoleWittenPhiRightTildeG.pdf}}}+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{TadpoleWittenPhiRightG_i.pdf}}}\\
&=-\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK^{w_{R}=1}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{R})\left(\lambda_{\Phi OO}\tilde{G}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{\Phi h_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)\right)\\
&=-\lambda_{\Phi OO}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK^{w_{R}=1}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{R})\left(\tilde{G}(X;X)-G_{\Delta}(X;X)\right)\\
&-\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK^{w_{R}=1}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{R})\left(\lambda_{\Phi OO}G_{\Delta}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{\Phi h_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)\right)\end{split} $$

where $h_{i}$ labels all fields in the bulk with homogeneous boundary conditions. Note that the term in the last line is just $\langle\Phi\rangle_{0,H^{d}}$ , the one-point function of a scalar in the UV theory on whole space, which is zero by conformal invariance. Then we may apply the identities (6.1) and (6.7) to the other term, which puts the bulk computation in a form closer to the CFT calculation:

$$ \begin{split}&\langle\Phi(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}=-\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\langle\sigma(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle_{H^{d}}\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\times\lambda_{\Phi OO}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK^{w_{R}=1}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{R})K^{w_{1}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})K^{w_{2}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{2}).\\
\end{split} $$

The integral in the last line is just the Witten diagram for propagators with homogeneous bulk boundary conditions, so it corresponds to a (Weyl-rescaled) three-point function in the UV theory on full space:

$$ \begin{split}&-2\lambda_{\Phi OO}^{\text{UV}}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK^{w_{R}=1}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{R})K^{w_{1}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})K^{w_{2}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{2})\\
&=\langle\Phi(x_{R})O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle_{0,H^{d}}\end{split} $$

The equivalence with the CFT calculation is clear (see eq. (2.29), and recall we need to perform a Weyl rescaling since we are working with $H^{d}$ at the boundary) :

$$ \begin{split}\langle\Phi(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}&=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}}{z_{1}^{d}z_{2}^{d}}(z_{1}z_{2})^{d-\Delta}\langle\sigma(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle z_{R}^{\Delta_{\Phi}}(z_{1}z_{2})^{\Delta}\langle\Phi(x_{R})O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle_{0}\\
&=z_{R}^{\Delta_{\Phi}}\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\langle\sigma(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle\langle\Phi(x_{R})O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle_{0}.\\
\end{split} $$

When $\Phi$ is placed on the unperturbed (“left”) side of the interface (at a point $x_{L}=(\mathbf{x}_{L},-z_{L})$ , $z_{L}>0$ ), we have

$$ \langle\Phi(x_{L})\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\langle\Phi(x_{L})O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle. $$

In this case, the corresponding tadpole Witten diagram is the same as (6.8) after replacing $K^{w=1}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}$ with $K^{w=0}_{\Delta_{\Phi}}$ . We can show the equivalence with the CFT calculation by applying the same identities that we used for the $\langle\Phi(x_{R})\rangle$ case.

#### 6.2.2 $\langle O\rangle$ and $\langle\sigma\rangle$

In the bulk, the tadpole Witten diagram that corresponds to the $O$ one-point function is

$$ \begin{split}&\langle O(x_{L})\rangle_{H^{d}}=\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{TadpoleWittenOLeftTildeG.pdf}}}+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{TadpoleWittenOLeftG_i.pdf}}}\\
&=-\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}X\tilde{K}_{w=0}(X;x_{L})\left(3\lambda_{OOO}\tilde{G}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{Oh_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)\right)\\
&=-3\lambda_{OOO}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}X\tilde{K}_{w=0}(X;x_{L})\left(\tilde{G}(X;X)-G_{\Delta}(X;X)\right)\\
&-\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta}(X;x_{L})\left(3\lambda_{OOO}G_{\Delta}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{Oh_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)\right)\\
&+\int_{H^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}\langle\sigma(x_{1})O(x_{L})\rangle\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})\left(3\lambda_{OOO}G_{\Delta}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{Oh_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)\right)\\
\end{split} $$

where we applied the identity (6.6). Note that the last two lines produce $\langle O\rangle_{0}$ upon integrating over the bulk, which is zero by conformal invariance. Then after applying the identities (6.1) and (6.7), we have

$$ \begin{split}&\langle O(x_{L})\rangle_{H^{d}}\\
&=-3\lambda_{OOO}\biggr[\int_{H^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}\langle\sigma(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle_{H^{d}}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta}(X;x_{L})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{2})\\
&-\int_{H^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}d^{d}x_{3}\langle\sigma(x_{1})O(x_{L})\rangle_{H^{d}}\langle\sigma(x_{2})\sigma(x_{3})\rangle_{H^{d}}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{2})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{3})\biggr]\end{split} $$

The integral in the last line is just the Witten diagram for propagators with homogeneous boundary conditions and relates to the corresponding CFT three-point function by

$$ \begin{split}&-6\lambda_{OOO}^{\text{UV}}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK^{w_{1}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})K^{w_{2}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{2})K^{w_{2}=1}_{\Delta}(X;x_{3})\\
&=\langle O(x_{1})O(x_{2})O(x_{3})\rangle_{0,H^{d}}\end{split} $$

This puts the bulk computation in an equivalent form as the CFT calculation, see eq. (2.33) (recall again that we are working in conventions where $C_{O}\equiv(2\Delta-d)\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}$ , as explained above).

The tadpole Witten diagram corresponding to the $\sigma$ one-point function to leading order at large $N$ is1414 14 There is a factor of $d-2\Delta$ on the LHS because of the differing normalizations between the field $\sigma$ defined on the CFT side (whose two-point function in the absence of the interface has a normalization given by $C_{\sigma}$ in (2.15)), and the operator $O_{d-\Delta}$ dual to the bulk scalar field with $d-\Delta$ boundary conditions, whose two-point function obtained from the bulk has the normalization (in the absence of the interface) $\langle O_{d-\Delta}(x_{1})O_{d-\Delta}(x_{2})\rangle=(d-2\Delta)\mathcal{C}_{d-\Delta}/x_{12}^{2(d-\Delta)}$ , see [22, 21]. The two operators are related by $O_{d-\Delta}=(d-2\Delta)\sigma$ .

$$ \begin{split}&(d-2\Delta)\langle\sigma(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}=\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{TadpoleWittenSigmaRightTildeG.pdf}}}+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{TadpoleWittenSigmaRightG_i.pdf}}}\\
\\
&=-\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}X\tilde{K}_{w=1}(X;x_{R})\left(3\lambda_{OOO}\tilde{G}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{\sigma h_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)\right)\\
&=(2\Delta-d)\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}X\int d^{d}x_{1}K_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})\langle\sigma(x_{1})\sigma(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}\\
&\qquad\times\left[3\lambda_{OOO}G_{\Delta}(X;X)+\sum_{h_{i}\neq\Delta}\lambda_{\sigma h_{i}h_{i}}G_{h_{i}}(X;X)+\frac{3\lambda_{OOO}}{d-2\Delta}\int d^{d}x_{2}\tilde{K}_{w=1}(X;x_{2})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{2})\right]\\
&=(2\Delta-d)3\lambda_{OOO}\int d^{d}x_{1}d^{d}x_{2}d^{d}x_{3}\langle\sigma(x_{R})\sigma(x_{1})\rangle\langle\sigma(x_{2})\sigma(x_{3})\rangle\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\times\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{2})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{3})\end{split} $$

where, as before, we applied the identities (6.1) and (6.7) and used the fact that $\langle O\rangle_{0}$ vanishes. After replacing the 3-point Witten diagram of homogeneous bulk-to-boundary propagators with its CFT equivalent (6.15), this again matches the CFT calculation in eq. (2.39).

### 6.3 Three-point functions

We also discuss equivalence of the three point functions $\langle\Phi\Phi O\rangle$ , $\langle\Phi OO\rangle$ , and $\langle OOO\rangle$ in AdS and CFT. From the CFT perspective, the three-point function $\langle\Phi\Phi O\rangle$ takes the form

$$ \begin{split}\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{L})\rangle&=\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{L})\rangle_{0}\\
&+\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}^{\prime}d^{d}x_{2}^{\prime}\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{1}^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle O(x_{L})O(x_{2}^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x_{1}^{\prime})\sigma(x_{2}^{\prime})\rangle\\
&=\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{L})\rangle_{0}-\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}^{\prime}\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{1}^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x_{1}^{\prime})O(x_{L})\rangle.\end{split} $$

In AdS, the three-point function is given by the Witten diagram

$$ \begin{split}&\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{L})\rangle_{H^{d}}=\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{ThreePointWittenPhiPhiO.pdf}}}\\
&=-2\lambda_{\Phi\Phi O}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{2})\tilde{K}_{w_{L}=0}(X;x_{L})\\
&=-2\lambda_{\Phi\Phi O}\biggr[\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{2})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{L})\\
&-\int_{H^{d}}\langle O(x_{L})\sigma(x^{\prime})\rangle_{H^{d}}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{2})K_{\Delta}^{w_{L}=0}(X;x_{L})\biggr]\end{split} $$

where we used identity (6.6) in the last equality. The remaining integrals over the AdS bulk are standard Witten diagrams corresponding to (Weyl-rescaled) three-point functions in the UV theory in the expected way

$$ \begin{split}&-2\lambda_{\Phi\Phi O}^{\text{UV}}\int_{H^{d+1}}d^{d+1}XK_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{2})K_{\Delta}(X;x_{R})\\
&=\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x_{R})\rangle_{0,H^{d}}\end{split} $$

The CFT calculation for $\langle\Phi\Phi\sigma\rangle$ is given by

$$ \begin{split}\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\sigma(x_{R})\rangle&=-\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x^{\prime}\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x^{\prime})\sigma(x_{R})\rangle\end{split} $$

The Witten diagram is given by

$$ \begin{split}&(d-2\Delta)\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\sigma(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}=\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[scale={.85}]{ThreePointWittenPhiPhiSigma.pdf}}}\\
&=-2\lambda_{\Phi\Phi O}\int_{H^{d+1}}K_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{1})K_{\Delta_{\Phi}}(X;x_{2})\tilde{K}_{w_{R}=1}(X;x_{R})\\
&=(2\Delta-d)\int_{H^{d}(w^{\prime}=1)}d^{d}x^{\prime}\langle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})O(x^{\prime})\rangle_{0,H^{d}}\langle\sigma(x^{\prime})\sigma(x_{R})\rangle_{H^{d}}\end{split} $$

where we used the relation between the UV CFT three point function and Witten diagram in the homogeneous theory given in (6.19). The CFT calculation for $\langle\Phi OO\rangle$ is given by

$$ \begin{split}&\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{L3})\rangle=\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{L3})\rangle_{0}\\
&+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}^{\prime}d^{d}x_{2}^{\prime}\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{L3})O(x_{1}^{\prime})O(x_{2}^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x_{1}^{\prime})\sigma(x_{2}^{\prime})\rangle\\
&+\frac{1}{4!}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}^{\prime}\dots d^{d}x_{4}^{\prime}\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{L3})O(x_{1}^{\prime})\dots O(x_{4}^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x_{1}^{\prime})\sigma(x_{2}^{\prime})\sigma(x_{3}^{\prime})\sigma(x_{4}^{\prime})\rangle.\end{split} $$

After Wick contractions and using the definition of $\langle O\sigma\rangle$ , we have

$$ \begin{split}\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{L3})\rangle&=\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{L3})\rangle_{0}\\
&-\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}d^{d}x_{1}^{\prime}\left[\langle\Phi(x_{1})O(x_{L2})O(x_{1}^{\prime})\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x_{1}^{\prime})O(x_{L3})\rangle+(L2\leftrightarrow L3)\right]\\

## Appendix A Two Point functions

### A.1 $\langle\sigma\sigma\rangle$

In this section we compute the sigma two-point function by inverting on half space the two-point function of $O$ from the UV theory on whole space. We have

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}dz\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}\langle O(x_{1})O(x)\rangle_{0}\langle\sigma(x)\sigma(x_{2})\rangle=-\delta^{d}(x_{1}-x_{2}) $$

where the correlation functions are constrained by conformal symmetry to take the form

$$ \langle O(x)O(x^{\prime})\rangle_{0}=\frac{C_{O}}{(x-x^{\prime})^{2\Delta}}\equiv\frac{g(\xi)}{(4zz^{\prime})^{\Delta}},\hskip 28.45274pt\langle\sigma(x)\sigma(x^{\prime})\rangle=\frac{h(\xi)}{(4zz^{\prime})^{d-\Delta}}. $$

We perform the inversion using the boundary CFT methods in [38, 51], which we review here. We would like to restate the inversion problem A.1 in terms of a single variable, so we first introduce another integral over coordinates parallel to the interface $\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}$ , giving

$$ \begin{split}\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}_{1}\int_{0}^{\infty}dz\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}\frac{g(\xi_{1})}{(4zz_{1})^{\Delta}}\frac{h(\xi_{2})}{(4zz_{2})^{d-\Delta}}&=-\delta(z_{1}-z_{2})\end{split} $$

where we defined

$$ \xi_{i}=\frac{(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i})^{2}+(z-z_{i})^{2}}{4zz_{i}},\qquad\rho_{i}=\frac{(z-z_{i})^{2}}{4zz_{i}}. $$

The act of integrating out $\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}$ corresponds to an integral transform, which has an inverse. We call this transform the “hat transform” and define it as follows

$$ \begin{split}\hat{f}(\rho_{1})&\equiv\frac{1}{(4zz_{1})^{(d-1)/2}}\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}f(\xi_{1})\\
&=\frac{\pi^{(d-1)/2}}{\Gamma(\tfrac{d-1}{2})}\int du\ u^{(d-3)/2}f(u+\rho_{1})\end{split} $$

The inverse of the hat transform is given by

$$ f(\xi_{1})=\frac{1}{\pi^{(d-1)/2}\Gamma(\tfrac{1-d}{2})}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\rho_{1}\ \rho_{1}^{-(d+1)/2}\hat{f}(\rho_{1}+\xi_{1}) $$

and this will be important for obtaining $\langle\sigma\sigma\rangle$ . The integrals over $\mathbf{x}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ produce the hat transforms of $g(\xi_{1})$ and $h(\xi)$ , so we have

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{2z}\hat{g}(\rho_{1})\hat{h}(\rho_{2})=-2z_{1}\delta(z_{1}-z_{2}). $$

We can then use a change of variables to rewrite the inversion problem in Eq. A.7 over positive $z$ as a convolution over the real line, which has a simple Fourier transform. Using the variables

$$ z_{1}=e^{2\theta_{1}},\hskip 14.22636ptz_{2}=e^{2\theta_{2}},\hskip 14.22636ptz=e^{2\theta} $$

Eq. A.7 becomes

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\theta\hat{g}(\sinh^{2}(\theta_{1}-\theta))\hat{h}(\sinh^{2}(\theta-\theta_{2}))=-\delta(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}). $$

Then Fourier transforming, we find that the Fourier transforms of $\hat{h}$ and $\hat{g}$ are related by

$$ \begin{split}\int d\theta_{12}d\theta e^{ik\theta_{12}}\hat{g}(\sinh^{2}(\theta_{12}-\theta))\hat{h}(\sinh^{2}(\theta))&=-1\\
\tilde{\hat{h}}(k)=-\frac{1}{\tilde{\hat{g}}(k)}.\end{split} $$

We can straightforwardly compute $\tilde{\hat{g}}(k)$ by applying the two integral transforms to $g(\xi)$ :

$$ \begin{split}&g(\xi)=\frac{C_{O}}{\xi^{\Delta}}\\
&\hat{g}(\rho)=\frac{C_{O}\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\rho^{\frac{1}{2}(d-2\Delta-1)}\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d}{2}+\Delta\right)}{\Gamma(\Delta)}\\
&\tilde{\hat{g}}(k)=\frac{C_{O}\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\Gamma\left(d-2\Delta\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d}{2}+\Delta\right)}{2^{d-2\Delta}\Gamma(\Delta)}\left(\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d+2\Delta}{2}-i\frac{k}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{1+d-2\Delta}{2}-i\frac{k}{2}\right)}+c.c.\right).\end{split} $$

Then $\tilde{\hat{h}}(k)$ is

$$ \tilde{\hat{h}}(k)=\frac{-2^{d-2\Delta-1}\Gamma(\Delta)}{C_{O}\pi^{\frac{d-3}{2}}\Gamma\left(d-2\Delta\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d}{2}+\Delta\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d+2\Delta-ik}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1-d+2\Delta+ik}{2}\right)\sin\pi\left(\frac{1-d+2\Delta}{2}\right)\cosh\left(\frac{\pi k}{2}\right)}. $$

Now we can work backwards to obtain the expression for $h(\xi)$ through an inverse Fourier transform followed by an inverse hat transform. The inverse Fourier transform can be computed by summing over residues of $k$ . We have

$$ \begin{split}&-\frac{\pi^{\frac{3}{2}-\frac{d}{2}}2^{d-2\Delta-1}\Gamma(\Delta)\sec\left(\frac{1}{2}\pi(d-2\Delta)\right)}{C_{O}\Gamma(d-2\Delta)\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\right)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}e^{-ik\theta}\frac{\text{sech}\left(\frac{\pi k}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\tfrac{-d-ik+1}{2}+\Delta\right)\Gamma\left(\tfrac{-d+ik+1}{2}+\Delta\right)}\\
&=-\frac{2\pi^{-\frac{d}{2}-1}e^{-\theta}\Gamma(\Delta)\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}\pi(d-2\Delta)\right)\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,\frac{1}{2}(d-2\Delta+2);-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+1;e^{-2\theta}\right)}{C_{O}\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)}\end{split} $$

After applying the hypergeometric identity1515 15 We are temporarily assuming $\theta>0$ , so $e^{-2\theta}<1$ and the identity is valid. We actually made this assumption when closing the contour in the lower half $k$ -plane in Eq. A.13, which converges for $\theta>0$ . If we instead consider $\theta<0$ and close the contour in the upper half plane of $k$ , the result contains a hypergeometric function with the same arguments, except for the last argument which is $e^{2\theta}$ instead of $e^{-2\theta}$ . Thus, the identity A.14 still applies, and in fact the final answer for $\hat{h}(\theta)$ is the same function for $\theta>0$ and $\theta<0$ .

$$ \,_{2}F_{1}(a,b;a-b+1;z)=(z+1)^{-a}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{a}{2},\frac{a+1}{2};a-b+1;\frac{4z}{(z+1)^{2}}\right),\qquad|z|<1 $$

$$ \begin{split}\hat{h}(\theta)&=-\frac{2\pi^{-\frac{d}{2}-1}e^{\theta}\Gamma(\Delta)\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}\pi(d-2\Delta)\right)\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{1}{2},1;-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+1;\text{sech}^{2}(\theta)\right)}{C_{O}\left(e^{2\theta}+1\right)\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)}\\

\end{split} $$

We now rewrite the hypergeometric function as a sum, apply the inverse hat transform, and perform the sum

$$ \begin{split}h(\xi)&=\frac{(d-2\Delta)\Gamma(\Delta)\sin\pi\left(\tfrac{d-2\Delta}{2}\right)}{2\pi^{d+1}C_{O}\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{2}\right)}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}+n+\Delta+1\right)}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\rho\rho^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}(1+\rho+\xi)^{-n-\frac{1}{2}}\\
&=\frac{\Gamma(\Delta)\sin\pi\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)}{C_{O}\pi^{d+1}\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)\xi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{d}{2},-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta,1-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta,-\frac{1}{\xi}\right).\end{split} $$

In the last line we used we used a hypergeometric identity1616 16 $\,{}_{2}F_{1}(a,b;c;z)=(1-z)^{-b}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(b,c-a;c;\frac{z}{z-1}\right)$ . The full result for the $\sigma$ propagator at leading order in large $N$ is thus

$$ \begin{split}\langle\sigma(x)\sigma(x^{\prime})\rangle&=\frac{h(\xi)}{(4zz^{\prime})^{d-\Delta}}\\
&=\frac{1}{(4zz^{\prime})^{d-\Delta}}\frac{\Gamma(\Delta)\sin\pi\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)}{C_{O}\pi^{d+1}\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)\xi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{d}{2},-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta,1-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta,-\frac{1}{\xi}\right).\end{split} $$

### A.2 $\langle O\sigma\rangle$

In this section we derive the correlator $\langle O(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle$ , where $x_{1}\in R_{-}^{d}$ and $x_{2}\in R_{+}^{d}$ are on opposite sides of the interface. We will work in the folded theory for convenience, taking $z_{1}\to-z_{1}$ and $\xi_{1}\to-(1+\xi_{1})$ . We can perform similar manipulations as in Appendix (A.1). The definition of $\langle O(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle_{\text{folded}}$ is

$$ \langle O(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle_{\text{folded}}=-\int_{0}^{\infty}dz\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}\langle O(x_{1})O(x)\rangle_{0,\text{folded}}\langle\sigma(x)\sigma(x_{2})\rangle $$

The correlators $\langle O\sigma\rangle_{\text{folded}}$ and $\langle OO\rangle_{\text{folded}}$ are constrained by conformal symmetry to take the form

$$ \langle O(x)\sigma(x^{\prime})\rangle_{\text{folded}}\equiv\frac{k(\xi)}{(2z)^{\Delta}(2z^{\prime})^{d-\Delta}},\hskip 28.45274pt\langle O(x)O(x^{\prime})\rangle_{0,\text{folded}}\equiv\frac{g_{f}(\xi)}{(4zz^{\prime})^{\Delta}}=\frac{C_{O}}{(4zz^{\prime})^{\Delta}}\frac{1}{(1+\xi)^{\Delta}} $$

while $\langle\sigma\sigma\rangle$ was just derived in A.17. Plugging this into A.18 and integrating both sides by $\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}_{1}$ gives

$$ \begin{split}\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}_{1}\frac{k(\xi_{12})}{(2z_{1})^{\Delta}(2z_{2})^{d-\Delta}}&=-\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}_{1}\int_{0}^{\infty}dz\int d^{d-1}\mathbf{x}\frac{g_{f}(\xi_{1})}{(4z_{1}z)^{\Delta}}\frac{h(\xi_{2})}{(4zz_{2})^{d-\Delta}}\\
\hat{k}(\rho_{12})&=-\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{2z}\hat{g}_{f}(\rho_{1})\hat{h}(\rho_{2}).\end{split} $$

where

$$ \rho_{12}=\frac{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}{4z_{1}z_{2}},\hskip 14.22636pt\rho_{1}=\frac{(z_{1}-z)^{2}}{4z_{1}z},\hskip 14.22636pt\rho_{2}=\frac{(z_{2}-z)^{2}}{4z_{2}z}. $$

Using the same change of variables as before

$$ z_{1}=e^{2\theta_{1}}\hskip 14.22636ptz_{2}=e^{2\theta_{2}}, $$

we have

$$ \hat{k}(\sinh^{2}\theta_{12})=-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\theta\ \hat{g}_{f}(\sinh^{2}(\theta_{12}-\theta))\hat{h}(\sinh^{2}(\theta)). $$

The Fourier transform over $\theta_{12}$ of this convolution is just

$$ \begin{split}\tilde{\hat{k}}(k)&=-\int d\theta_{12}e^{ik\theta_{12}}\int d\theta\ \hat{g}_{f}(\sinh^{2}(\theta_{12}-\theta))\hat{h}(\sinh^{2}(\theta))\\
&=-\tilde{\hat{g}}_{f}(k)\tilde{\hat{h}}(k).\end{split} $$

While $\tilde{\hat{h}}(k)$ is given in A.12, we still need to compute $\tilde{\hat{g}}_{f}(k)$ by applying a hat transform and Fourier transform. We have

$$ \begin{split}g_{f}(\xi)&=\frac{1}{(1+\xi)^{\Delta}}\\
\hat{g}_{f}(\rho)&=\frac{C_{O}\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma(\Delta)}(\rho+1)^{\frac{1}{2}(d-2\Delta-1)}\\
\tilde{\hat{g}}_{f}(k)&=\frac{\text{Co}\pi^{d/2}\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}(-d-ik+1)+\Delta\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}(-d+ik+1)+\Delta\right)}{\Gamma(\Delta)\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+1\right)}\end{split} $$

In the last line we used the following result

$$ \begin{split}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\theta\ e^{ik\theta}(\cosh^{2}(\theta))^{\frac{d-2\Delta-1}{2}}&=\frac{2\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,\frac{1}{2}(d+ik-2\Delta+1);\frac{1}{2}(-d+ik+3)+\Delta;-1\right)}{-d+2\Delta+ik+1}\\
&\qquad-\frac{2\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,\frac{1}{2}(d-ik-2\Delta+1);\frac{1}{2}(-d-ik+3)+\Delta;-1\right)}{d-2\Delta+ik-1}\\
&=\frac{2^{2\Delta-d}\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}-\frac{ik}{2}+\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(-\frac{d}{2}+\frac{ik}{2}+\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma(-d+2\Delta+1)}\end{split} $$

where we applied the hypergeometric identity

$$ \begin{split}\,{}_{2}F_{1}(a,b;c;z)&=\frac{(-z)^{-a}\Gamma(c)\Gamma(b-a)\,_{2}F_{1}\left(a,a-c+1;a-b+1;\frac{1}{z}\right)}{\Gamma(b)\Gamma(c-a)}\\

to the second hypergeometric function in the first line of A.26. Plugging the results for $\tilde{\hat{g}}_{f}$ and $\tilde{\hat{h}}$ into A.24, we have simply

$$ \begin{split}\tilde{\hat{k}}(k)&=\sin\pi(\tfrac{d}{2}-\Delta)\text{sech}\left(\tfrac{\pi k}{2}\right).\end{split} $$

It is then straightforward to compute the inverse Fourier transform and inverse hat transform:

$$ \begin{split}\hat{k}(\rho)&=\frac{\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}\pi(d-2\Delta)\right)}{\pi\sqrt{\rho+1}}\\

So the final result for the $\langle O\sigma\rangle$ correlator is given by

$$ \begin{split}\langle O(x_{1})\sigma(x_{2})\rangle_{\text{folded}}&=\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\sin\pi\left(\frac{d}{2}-\Delta\right)}{\pi^{d/2+1}(2z_{1})^{\Delta}(2z_{2})^{d-\Delta}(1+\xi_{12})^{\frac{d}{2}}}\\

### A.3 $\langle OO\rangle$

Starting from the $O\sigma$ two point function we now look at deriving the $\langle O(x_{1})O(x_{2})\rangle$ correlator on the UV side of the interface. Again, we use the folded theory for convenience and take $z_{1}\to-z_{1}$ , $z_{2}\to-z_{2}$ :

Since $\langle OO\rangle$ is constrained by conformal symmetry, the second term of A.31 must take the form

where we plugged in $\tilde{\hat{g}}(k)$ and $\tilde{\hat{k}}(k)$ from A.25 and A.29. We can perform the inverse Fourier transform by summing over residues1717 17 Note that the comment in footnote 15 also applies here.

$$ \begin{split}\hat{l}(\rho)&=-\frac{C_{O}\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\Gamma\left(\Delta+\frac{1-d}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\Delta\right)\rho^{\Delta+\frac{1-d}{2}}}+\frac{C_{O}\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\Delta)\Gamma(1+\tfrac{d}{2}-\Delta)\rho^{1/2}}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{d}{2}-\Delta;\frac{d}{2}-\Delta+1;-\frac{1}{\rho}\right)\\

where we applied hypergeometric identities A.14 and

$$ \,_{2}F_{1}(a,b;c;z)=(1-z)^{-a}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(a,c-b;c;\frac{z}{z-1}\right) $$

to simplify the expression. Then applying the inverse hat transform gives

$$ l(\xi)=-\frac{C_{O}}{\xi^{\Delta}}+\frac{C_{O}\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{d}{2},\frac{1}{2}(d-2\Delta);\frac{1}{2}(d-2\Delta+2);-\frac{1}{\xi}\right)}{\Gamma(\Delta)\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}-\Delta+1\right)\xi^{d/2}} $$

$$ \begin{split}&\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\theta e^{ik\theta}\left(\sinh^{2}\left(\theta\right)-w_{1}+1\right){}^{\frac{1}{2}(d-2\Delta-1)}\\
&=\frac{2^{2\Delta-d}\Gamma\left(\tfrac{-d-ik+2\Delta+1}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\tfrac{-d+ik+2\Delta+1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma(-d+2\Delta+1)}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-\frac{d}{2}-\frac{ik}{2}+\Delta+\frac{1}{2},&-\frac{d}{2}+\frac{ik}{2}+\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\\
-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+1&\end{array}\biggr|w_{1}\right).\end{split} $$

The Fourier transform of the LHS can be found in a similar way, which leads to the expression

$$ \begin{split}&\pi\text{sech}\left(\frac{\pi k}{2}\right)\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{-d-ik+1}{2}+\Delta,\frac{-d+ik+1}{2}+\Delta;-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+1;w_{1}\right)\\
&=-A\frac{\pi^{-d/2}\Gamma(\Delta)}{C_{O}\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)}\text{sech}\left(\frac{\pi k}{2}\right)\,_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{-d-ik+1}{2}+\Delta,\frac{-d+ik+1}{2}+\Delta;-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta+1;w_{1}\right).\end{split} $$

This is true for

$$ A=-\frac{\pi^{d/2}C_{O}\Gamma\left(\Delta-\frac{d}{2}\right)}{\Gamma(\Delta)}\equiv-\frac{C_{O}}{\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}}. $$

Thus, we have shown the identity is correct and takes the form

$$ \begin{split}&\tilde{K}(w_{1},x_{1};w_{2}=1,x_{2})\\
&=-\frac{C_{O}}{\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}}\int_{H^{d}(w=1)}d^{d}x\sqrt{g}K_{\Delta}(w_{1},x_{1};w=1,x)(zz_{2})^{d-\Delta}\langle\sigma(x)\sigma(x_{2})\rangle.\end{split} $$
